{{Short description|Inequality of acute angles and their trigonometric ratios}}
{{one source |date=May 2024}}
'''Aristarchus's inequality''' (after the Greek [[Ancient Greek astronomy|astronomer]] and [[Greek mathematics|mathematician]] [[Aristarchus of Samos]]; c. 310 – c. 230 BCE) is a law of [[trigonometry]] which states that if ''&alpha;'' and ''&beta;'' are [[acute angle]]s (i.e.&nbsp;between 0 and a right angle) and ''&beta;''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''&alpha;'' then

: <math> \frac{\sin\alpha}{\sin\beta} < \frac{\alpha}{\beta} < \frac{\tan\alpha}{\tan\beta}. </math>

[[Ptolemy]] used the first of these inequalities while constructing [[Ptolemy's table of chords|his table of chords]].<ref name=toomer>{{Citation|title=Ptolemy's Almagest|last1=Toomer|first1=G. J.|authorlink=Gerald J. Toomer|publisher=Princeton University Press|page= 54|year= 1998|ISBN =0-691-00260-6}}</ref>

== Proof ==
The proof is a consequence of the more widely known inequalities

:<math> 0<\sin(\alpha)<\alpha<\tan(\alpha) </math>,

:<math> 0<\sin(\beta)<\sin(\alpha)<1 </math> and 

:<math> 1>\cos(\beta)>\cos(\alpha)>0</math>.

=== Proof of the first inequality ===
Using these inequalities we can first prove that

: <math> \frac{\sin(\alpha)}{\sin(\beta)} < \frac{\alpha}{\beta}. </math>

We first note that the inequality is equivalent to
:<math>\frac{\sin(\alpha)}{\alpha} < \frac{\sin(\beta)}{\beta} </math>
which itself can be rewritten as
:<math>\frac{\sin(\alpha)-\sin(\beta)}{\alpha-\beta} < \frac{\sin(\beta)}{\beta}. </math>

We now want to show that
:<math>\frac{\sin(\alpha)-\sin(\beta)}{\alpha-\beta}<\cos(\beta) < \frac{\sin(\beta)}{\beta}. </math>

The second inequality is simply <math>\beta<\tan\beta</math>. The first one is true because
: <math> 
\frac{\sin(\alpha)-\sin(\beta)}{\alpha-\beta}
= \frac{2\cdot\sin\left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}2
\right)\cos\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\right)}{\alpha-\beta}
< \frac{2\cdot \left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}2
\right) \cdot \cos(\beta)}{\alpha-\beta}
= \cos(\beta).
</math>

=== Proof of the second inequality ===

Now we want to show the second inequality, i.e. that:

: <math> \frac{\alpha}{\beta} <\frac{\tan(\alpha)}{\tan(\beta)}. </math>

We first note that due to the initial inequalities we have that:

:<math> \beta<\tan(\beta)=\frac{\sin(\beta)}{\cos(\beta)}<\frac{\sin(\beta)}{\cos(\alpha)} </math>

Consequently, using that <math>0<\alpha-\beta<\alpha </math> in the previous equation (replacing <math>\beta </math> by <math>\alpha-\beta<\alpha </math>) we obtain:
: <math>{\alpha-\beta}<{\frac{\sin(\alpha-\beta)}{\cos(\alpha)}}=\tan(\alpha)\cos(\beta)-\sin(\beta).</math>
We conclude that
: <math> \frac{\alpha}{\beta}=\frac{\alpha-\beta}{\beta}+1< \frac{\tan(\alpha)\cos(\beta)-\sin(\beta)}{\sin(\beta)}+1 = \frac{\tan(\alpha)}{\tan(\beta)}. </math>
